My heart slams, I can’t breathe, I sweat out of nowhere, and sometimes I feel like I’m going to pass out. It’s gotten so I avoid anything medical. I skipped my physical this year and I white-knuckle it during flu season.

It’s funny—this never used to bother me. Maybe it started around the time of… well, an incident last year. I was in the parking garage after work when something happened—nothing violent, just scary. I’d rather not say more. But since then, I notice I’m more jumpy, and my body seems to react to things faster, like it’s on high alert sometimes. But I don’t have nightmares or constantly think about it—I’m not *that* out of control. Still, when it comes to blood or needles, my body just… overreacts.

I wasn’t physically hurt, but seeing all the blood… it stuck with me. 

Since then, even the sight of a small cut or someone getting a flu shot makes my heart race, I start sweating, my breath gets shallow, and sometimes I feel like I’m going to pass out. Once, I nearly collapsed during a routine blood draw at the clinic. The nurse had to lay me down. I’ve started avoiding any medical appointments, which is starting to worry me, especially with my family history.

I don’t have nightmares about the accident, and I’m not constantly on edge. I don’t avoid driving or revisiting the area where it happened. It’s just blood and needles—those specific things set off this intense physical reaction. Everything else in my life feels under control—my job, my marriage—but this one thing has me stuck.
D012-D018_h001.question_b: I’ve always been a bit uneasy around needles, but everything changed after my car accident last year—being trapped in the wreckage, bleeding, watching blood everywhere… ever since, it’s like something snapped. The worst part isn’t just the panic—it’s that the accident replays in my head constantly. I keep seeing the shattered windshield, hearing the crunch of metal. I don’t sleep through the night. I’m jumpy, irritable, avoid the news, avoid hospitals, even skip check-ups. At first I thought it was just the fear of needles, but it’s not just medical stuff—I’m haunted. D012-D018_h019.question_both:
I’ve always been careful, detail-oriented—part of the job when you spend hours peering through a loupe at gem inclusions. But over the past few months, something’s shifted, though I can’t pinpoint when exactly. There’s this... dread around certain animals. Spiders, mostly. Even pictures of them make my chest tighten, my hands go clammy, like I can’t catch my breath. Once, during an estate appraisal, I saw one in the corner of an old jewelry box—just a tiny house spider—and my heart started hammering so hard I had to sit down. I couldn’t move until my assistant came in and cleared it.

Now, I won’t go into basements or attic inventories alone. I bring a colleague, or I ask the owner to check first. Carrying a flashlight, keeping my sleeves down—it helps, just enough to get through the day. There was an incident years ago, out hiking—something happened with wildlife, I don’t like to talk about it. But I don’t even know if that’s connected. I sleep okay, mostly. No nightmares, not really. Just this constant, low hum of alertness around certain things. Like my body remembers something my mind won’t.
D012-D018_h019.question_a:
I’ve always loved my work as a gemologist—spending hours leaning over jewels with a loupe, the quiet focus of it. But for the past three years, ever since a bad incident on a hike where a large spider crawled on me, I can’t seem to shake this overwhelming fear of spiders. Even seeing a tiny one in the corner of my apartment sends my heart racing, my palms sweating, and sometimes I feel like I can’t catch my breath—like I’m going to pass out. 

I won’t go into basements or attics alone, and if I have to enter a room that’s been closed off, I make sure a friend is with me. Just having someone nearby makes it barely bearable. I know it sounds irrational—spiders aren’t everywhere, and most are harmless—but my body reacts like it’s life or death.

I didn’t develop nightmares or flashbacks from the hike, and aside from this one fear, I haven’t felt hypervigilant or emotionally numb since. It’s just spiders—intense, paralyzing fear, and nothing else.
D012-D018_h019.question_b:
I’ve always worked alone—being a gemologist means long hours inspecting stones under magnification, just me and my tools. But about six months ago, after I was attacked by a stray dog while walking home, everything changed. I didn’t just get bitten—there was a lot of blood, I couldn’t breathe, I thought I was going to die.  

Since then, I can’t be near any dogs, not even small ones. Just seeing one across the street makes my heart race, my palms sweat, I start trembling like I’m back in that moment. Sometimes I feel like I’m reliving it—the sound of the snarling, the pain. I avoid certain neighborhoods entirely, take long detours, and if I have to go somewhere new, I only do it if a friend walks with me. I carry pepper spray everywhere, like a security blanket.  

But it’s not just the dog fear. I keep having nightmares about the attack. I’m jumpy all the time, can’t focus at work. I even flinch when someone’s phone rings too loud—it reminds me of the dog lunging. It’s like the whole world feels dangerous now. This isn’t just about dogs—it’s like my brain won’t let me move past what happened.

I’ve been like this for a while now—can’t say exactly how long, maybe a couple of years? Ever since that accident with the tractor… well, I don’t like to talk much about it. But ever since then, certain things just set me off. Loud noises—sudden ones, like a backfire or a burst pipe—send a shock through me. My chest tightens, I can’t breathe right, like I’m trapped in that moment. It’s not every sound, mind you—just the sharp ones, the unexpected.  

I won’t go to town on market day anymore. Too many tractors, too many chances for that bang. If I have to go somewhere noisy, my wife comes with me. Just having her there helps. I know she’ll notice if something’s coming, give me a heads-up. Without her, I don’t think I could do it.  

Sometimes I see the machine flipping over in my head—even when it’s quiet. Not often, not like some folks probably get, but enough. I don’t dream about it regularly or anything. I just… avoid what I can. Can’t afford to fall apart. There’s work to do. But some days, even the wind through the silo sounds too much like metal twisting.
D012-D018_h020.question_a:
I’ve been a farmer my whole life, and up until a few years ago, I never had any issues being around animals. But after a bull attacked me—gored my leg pretty bad—I can’t even go near one now. The moment I see a bull, even from a distance, my heart slams in my chest, I can’t breathe, and I start shaking like I’m back in that pen. It’s like my body just takes over and screams *run*. My wife says I turn white as a sheet.

I only make it to the far pasture if my son goes with me. I won’t go alone—just knowing he’s there, watching my back, is the only thing that keeps me from panicking completely. I’ve even avoided checking on some of the livestock because of it. It’s affecting my work, and that’s not like me.

Now, I do have the memory of the attack—I think about it sometimes, especially when I’m near the pens—but I don’t have nightmares or flashbacks, and I’m not jumpy all the time. It’s just the bulls. That’s it. The fear is sharp, but only when I’m facing them.
D012-D018_h020.question_b: I’ve been having these terrible reactions ever since that accident last year—got caught in a flash flood while checking irrigation lines. Water surged outta nowhere, dragged me fifty yards, I nearly drowned. Since then, any loud noise—like thunder or even a truck backfiring—sends me into a panic. My heart slams, I can’t breathe, feel like I’m back in the current. I won’t go into town alone now. My wife has to come with me, or I carry that old walkie-talkie I used during the flood—just having it in my hand helps a little. But it’s not just about noise or water anymore. I keep reliving it: nightmares two, three times a week, can’t get the image outta my head. I’m jumpy all the time, don’t sleep well, stay on edge even out in the fields. I used to love working alone at dawn. Now I don’t feel safe anywhere unless she’s near. It’s like the whole world’s too loud, too fast. And I just can’t seem to shake that moment—it’s like it never left.

- Natural Environment Type (Marked fear of the natural environment like storms, heights, water, or the dark.)

**Ambiguity Logic Constraints (CRITICAL - The "Void" Logic):**
- **Goal:** Create a scenario where a definitive diagnosis is IMPOSSIBLE based on the text provided.

- **Constraint:** DO NOT include any pathognomonic features (determining symptoms) that would confirm A or B. Keep the severity and duration strictly in the "gray zone".
